curriculum.lesson_evidence: A prototype is a quick cardboard model built to learn, not the finished organiser you hope to keep. The final idea states what the organiser should do: hold 8 pencils, fit the 15 cm corner, and have smooth edges, using the standing roll with a wider base. The prototype simplifies that idea so it can be tried today with scrap card and scissors. It may be rougher, shorter or joined with simple slots. Its job is to answer the criteria, not to look neat. Refusing to build until the drawing looks perfect stops you learning. Calling the rough model “finished forever” stops you improving it.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Write two short parts for Jordan: what the final standing-roll idea promises, and what the cardboard prototype simplifies so it can be tested today with scrap card and scissors. Keep an adult nearby for cutting.

FEEDBACK
The final roll promises eight pencils, a 15 cm corner fit and smooth edges on a wider base. The prototype uses scrap cardboard and slotted tabs, may be shorter or rougher, and exists so those checks can be tried. Looking neat is not the prototype’s job. Scissors remain the only cutter, with an adult nearby. The rough tube is a test piece, not the final organiser.

WATCH FOR
Treating the first rough cardboard tube as the final product, or waiting for a perfect drawing before any model. A prototype is allowed to look unfinished because its job is to answer a test. A final idea is the promise you are aiming at. Keep the two descriptions separate.
